header.title: Pressure & Partial Pressure
header.subtitle: Understanding how pressure changes with depth and affects the gases you breathe

reading.title: Reading a Dive Profile
reading.text: A dive profile is a graphical representation of your dive, showing depth over time. Understanding the basic terminology helps you communicate with other divers and interpret dive computer data effectively.

descent.label: Descent
descent.text: The phase from leaving the surface until reaching your planned depth. Recommended rate: ≤18-20 m/min.

bottomTime.label: Bottom Time
bottomTime.text: Total time from beginning of descent to start of final ascent. Includes descent phase.

maxDepth.label: Maximum Depth
maxDepth.text: The deepest point reached during the dive. Determines ambient pressure and gas absorption rate.

ascent.label: Ascent
ascent.text: Return to surface. Rate should not exceed 9-10 m/min to prevent bubble formation.

tdt.label: Total Dive Time (TDT)
tdt.text: Complete duration from leaving surface to returning. Includes descent, bottom time, and full ascent.

decoStop.label: Deco Stop
decoStop.text: Mandatory pause at specific depth during ascent to allow safe elimination of inert gases.

safetyStop.label: Safety Stop
safetyStop.text: Voluntary 3-minute pause at 3-5m during ascent to allow excess nitrogen to off-gas safely.

surfaceInterval.label: Surface Interval (SI)
surfaceInterval.text: Time spent at surface between dives to off-gas nitrogen. Longer SI = more nitrogen eliminated.

whatCreates.title: What Creates Pressure Underwater?
whatCreates.intro: The total pressure a diver experiences underwater comes from two sources:
whatCreates.atmospheric: Atmospheric pressure — The weight of the air column above you. At sea level, this is approximately 1 bar (1 atm = 1.01325 bar).
whatCreates.hydrostatic: Hydrostatic pressure — The weight of the water column above you. In seawater, this adds approximately 1 bar per 10 meters of depth.
whatCreates.summary: Therefore, at 10m depth you experience 2 bar total pressure (1 atm + 1 bar water), at 20m it's 3 bar, at 30m it's 4 bar, and so on.

altitude.intro: Atmospheric pressure decreases with altitude. If you dive in a mountain lake, you start with less than 1 bar at the surface:
altitude.note: ⚠️ Altitude diving requires special procedures and decompression adjustments.

formulas.totalAmbientDesc: The total pressure at any depth is the sum of atmospheric and hydrostatic pressure:
formulas.pAtm: atmospheric pressure (≈1 bar at sea level)
formulas.simplifiedDesc: For diving at sea level, we use the simplified formula:
formulas.simplifiedNote: This approximation works well for recreational diving calculations.
formulas.altitudeFormulaDesc: Atmospheric pressure decreases exponentially with altitude:

whyDepth.title: Why Depth Matters for Gas Supply
whyDepth.text1: According to Boyle-Mariotte's Law, as pressure increases, the volume of gas decreases proportionally. Underwater, this means you breathe compressed air from your tank. At 10m depth (2 bar), each breath draws twice the amount of gas molecules compared to the surface.
whyDepth.text2: This is why deeper dives consume your gas supply faster—you're breathing the same volume of air, but it contains more gas molecules due to compression.

sac.title: Surface Air Consumption (SAC)
sac.text1: SAC rate (also called RMV - Respiratory Minute Volume) is how much gas you breathe per minute at the surface. For planning purposes, we use a typical value of 20 L/min for relaxed diving, though actual consumption varies based on exertion, stress, and individual factors.
sac.text2: At depth, your actual consumption is: SAC × Ambient Pressure

formula.consumedDesc: The gas consumption at any depth can be calculated as:
formula.availableExample: For a 12L cylinder at 200 bar with 50 bar reserve:

sacCalc.intro: Knowing your personal SAC rate helps you plan dives more accurately. You can calculate it from real dive data using your pressure drop, cylinder size, dive time, and average depth.
sacCalc.deltaP: Pressure drop (start - end pressure in bar)
sacCalc.examplePressure: Start pressure: 200 bar, End pressure: 80 bar → ΔP = 120 bar
sacCalc.showSolution: Try it yourself first — click to reveal the solution
sacCalc.exampleResult: This diver has a SAC rate of 12.8 L/min — quite efficient! Typical recreational divers range from 12-25 L/min depending on fitness, experience, and conditions.
sacCalc.tip1: Use a dive computer that logs average depth, or calculate it from your profile
sacCalc.tip2: Measure over several dives to get a reliable average
sacCalc.tip3: Note that SAC increases with exertion, cold, or stress
sacCalc.tip4: For planning, use a conservative (higher) SAC estimate

whatsInAir.title: What's in the Air You Breathe?
whatsInAir.intro: The air we breathe is a mixture of gases. Understanding this composition is fundamental to diving because each gas behaves differently under pressure. The main components are:
whatsInAir.nitrogen: Nitrogen (N₂) — 78% — inert gas, does not participate in metabolism
whatsInAir.oxygen: Oxygen (O₂) — 21% — essential for life, but toxic at high partial pressures
whatsInAir.other: Other gases — 1% — primarily Argon, CO₂, and trace gases

mixtures.title: Breathing Gas Mixtures
mixtures.intro: Divers use different gas mixtures to manipulate the partial pressures of specific gases at depth. By changing the fraction of each gas in a mix, divers can stay within safe limits for oxygen toxicity and nitrogen narcosis:
mixtures.nitrox: Nitrox (EAN) — Increases the oxygen fraction to lower the partial pressure of nitrogen (ppN2), which reduces nitrogen loading in the tissues.
mixtures.trimix: Trimix — Adds helium to the mix, allowing divers to lower the partial pressures of both oxygen and nitrogen to safe levels for deep diving.

foundation.title: The Foundation of Dive Gas Physics
foundation.text: Dalton's Law states that the total pressure of a gas mixture equals the sum of the partial pressures of each component gas. The partial pressure of a gas is the pressure it would exert if it occupied the same volume alone.

animation.caption: Each gas (blue, red) exerts its own pressure independently — the total pressure is the sum of all partial pressures.

formula.fx: fraction of gas x in the mixture (decimal, e.g., 0.21 for 21%)
formula.note: Note: This is the operational formula used for MOD and gas limits throughout this section.

example.intro: At 30 meters, the ambient pressure is 4 bar (1 + 30/10). For air:

operational.title: Operational vs Physiological Partial Pressure
operational.intro: There are two common contexts for partial pressure calculations:
operational.opDesc: Used for Maximum Operating Depth (MOD) and oxygen toxicity limits. No water vapour subtraction.
operational.physDesc: When calculating alveolar gas pressures for tissue loading models, we subtract water vapour pressure because the lungs humidify inspired air:
operational.physNote: This ~6% reduction appears in the Bühlmann equations for tissue saturation calculations. We will need this in further sections and stating it here for completeness.

oxygenLimits.title: Oxygen Limits (ppO₂)
oxygenLimits.intro: Oxygen becomes toxic at elevated partial pressures. The body responds differently to various ppO₂ levels:
oxygenLimits.hypoxiaNotes: Loss of consciousness, death. Minimum for survival.
oxygenLimits.safeNotes: Recommended working limit for recreational diving.
oxygenLimits.cautionNotes: Acceptable for decompression stops only. Limited exposure time.
oxygenLimits.dangerNotes: High risk of CNS oxygen toxicity (seizures).

mod.title: Maximum Operating Depth (MOD)
mod.intro: The MOD is the deepest you can safely dive with a specific gas mix without exceeding the ppO₂ limit. It's calculated from the oxygen fraction and desired maximum ppO₂.
mod.exerciseNote: 💡 Notice: higher O₂ fraction → shallower MOD. More oxygen means you hit the toxicity limit sooner.

nitrogenLimits.title: Nitrogen Limits (ppN₂) — Narcosis
nitrogenLimits.intro: Nitrogen becomes narcotic at elevated partial pressures, causing impaired judgment, euphoria, and slowed reactions—similar to alcohol intoxication.
nitrogenLimits.martiniIntro: A popular rule of thumb: every 10 meters of depth on air is roughly equivalent to drinking one martini on an empty stomach. At 30m, you might feel like you've had 3 martinis!
nitrogenLimits.martiniNote: Note: Individual susceptibility varies greatly. Some divers feel effects earlier, others later. Cold, stress, and fatigue increase narcosis.
nitrogenLimits.severe: Severe narcosis. Maximum limit for recreational diving.
nitrogenLimits.exercisesTitle: Exercises: Max depth for narcosis limit
nitrogenLimits.strictNote: ← stricter limit used by some training agencies
nitrogenLimits.exercisesHint: Same formula as MOD, but for nitrogen: Max depth = ((ppN₂<sub>max</sub> / fN₂) − 1) × 10
nitrogenLimits.exerciseNote: 💡 Nitrox pushes the narcosis limit deeper, but the oxygen MOD kicks in first — you always need to respect both limits. The actual limiting factor for EAN mixes is usually oxygen, not narcosis.

twoTypes.title: Two Types of Oxygen Toxicity
twoTypes.intro: Breathing oxygen at elevated partial pressures can cause two distinct types of toxicity:

cnsOtu.title: CNS & OTU Tracking
cnsOtu.disclaimer: ⚠️ This is advanced content. For recreational diving, simply staying below 1.4 bar ppO₂ is sufficient. CNS/OTU tracking is primarily used in technical diving with extended oxygen exposures.
cnsOtu.cnsDesc: The CNS clock tracks your exposure as a percentage of the maximum allowable time at each ppO₂ level. At 100%, you've reached the recommended limit.
cnsOtu.otuDesc: OTU tracks cumulative pulmonary (lung) oxygen exposure. The formula applies when ppO₂ exceeds 0.5 bar:
cnsOtu.otuLimits: Daily limits: 300 OTU (single dive), 850 OTU (total daily)

symptoms.title: Symptoms of CNS Oxygen Toxicity
symptoms.warning: ⚠️ If you experience any of these symptoms, immediately signal your buddy and begin ascending. Underwater convulsions are often fatal.

header.title: Tissue Loading & Saturation
header.subtitle: Visualize how nitrogen saturates and desaturates in your body during a dive

whyMatters.title: Why Does This Matter?
whyMatters.text: When you dive, the increased pressure causes nitrogen from the air you breathe to dissolve into your body tissues. The deeper you go and the longer you stay, the more nitrogen accumulates. If you ascend too quickly, this nitrogen can form bubbles in your tissues — causing decompression sickness (DCS), also known as "the bends."

henrysLaw.title: Henry's Law: Gas Dissolution
henrysLaw.text1: Henry's Law states that the amount of gas dissolved in a liquid is proportional to the pressure of that gas above the liquid. Think of a soda bottle: when sealed under pressure, CO₂ stays dissolved. Open the cap (reduce pressure), and bubbles form as gas comes out of solution.
henrysLaw.text2: The same principle applies to your body during a dive. As you descend and pressure increases, more gas dissolves into your blood and tissues. While this applies to all gases you breathe, oxygen (O₂) is not a concern for bubble formation because:
henrysLaw.o2reason1: Your body continuously consumes oxygen through metabolism
henrysLaw.o2reason2: Most oxygen in blood is bound to hemoglobin in red blood cells, not freely dissolved
henrysLaw.text3: The gas we must carefully manage is nitrogen (N₂) — it's inert (your body doesn't use it) and makes up 78% of air. For technical divers using trimix, helium (He) follows the same principles but with different solubility characteristics.
henrysLaw.footnote: Notice that fatty tissues can hold 5× more nitrogen than blood at the same pressure!

gasExchange.title: Gas Exchange Pathway
gasExchange.intro: Gas flows along the partial pressure gradient — from higher pressure to lower pressure. During a dive, the pathway is:

svg.flowDirection: → Gas flows from HIGH to LOW pressure

alveolarFormula.desc: The partial pressure of nitrogen in the alveoli accounts for water vapor pressure:
alveolarFormula.fN2: fraction of nitrogen in breathing gas (0.79 for air)

saturationDynamics.title: Saturation Dynamics During a Dive
saturationDynamics.intro: Understanding how tissue loading changes throughout a dive is key to safe decompression:

descent.heading: ⬇️ a) Descent — On-gassing
descent.text: As you descend, ambient pressure increases. The partial pressure of nitrogen in your lungs becomes higher than in your tissues, so gas flows into tissues. All compartments begin absorbing nitrogen, but fast tissues fill first.

atDepth.heading: ➡️ b) At Depth — Differential Saturation
atDepth.text: While at your maximum depth, fast tissues approach equilibrium within minutes. Medium tissues continue loading. Slow tissues (like fat) are still far from saturation — they would need hours at depth to fully equilibrate.

ascent.heading: ⬆️ c) Ascent — Off-gassing & Supersaturation
ascent.text1: As you ascend, the partial pressure of nitrogen in your lungs drops. When tissue nitrogen pressure exceeds alveolar pressure, the gradient reverses and gas flows out — this is off-gassing.
ascent.text2: But there's another threshold: when tissue nitrogen pressure exceeds ambient pressure, the tissue is supersaturated. This is when we need to be careful — the dissolved gas wants to come out of solution and could form bubbles.

critical.heading: ⚠️ Critical Supersaturation
critical.text1: Some supersaturation is tolerable — our bodies can handle a certain amount of excess dissolved gas without forming bubbles. However, if tissues become too supersaturated, dissolved nitrogen can form bubbles instead of diffusing out safely.
critical.text2: The maximum tolerable supersaturation is called critical supersaturation — it varies by tissue type and depth. In the next chapter, we'll explore how to calculate these limits.

bubbleMechanics.title: What Happens to Bubbles During Ascent?
bubbleMechanics.intro: A gas bubble in tissue has three pressures acting on it:
bubbleMechanics.pSurface: Surface tension (2γ/r) — the Laplace pressure, also squeezes the bubble. Smaller bubbles have more surface tension.
bubbleMechanics.pTissue: Dissolved gas tension (Ptissue) — the total pressure of gases dissolved in surrounding tissue, pushing gas into the bubble
bubbleMechanics.insight: When Ptissue > Pamb + 2γ/r, gas diffuses into the bubble and it grows. As it grows, r increases, surface tension drops, making growth even easier — a positive feedback loop.
bubbleMechanics.sliderHint: Use the slider to ascend from 30m. Watch how reducing ambient pressure tips the balance — larger bubbles cross the critical radius first.

halfTimeConcept.title: The Half-Time Concept
halfTimeConcept.intro: We've seen what happens during on-gassing and off-gassing — now let's explore how these processes unfold over time. Like radioactive decay and many other natural phenomena, gas diffusion in tissues follows a predictable mathematical pattern.
halfTimeConcept.definition: A tissue's half-time is how long it takes to become 50% saturated (or 50% desaturated) at a given pressure difference. After each half-time period:
halfTimeConcept.example: A 5-minute compartment reaches 50% saturation in 5 minutes; a 635-minute compartment takes over 10 hours!
halfTimeConcept.gradientText1: A tissue's half-time is constant — it always takes the same time to close 50% of the gap between current tissue pressure and the target. But when that gap is larger, 50% represents more gas in absolute terms.
halfTimeConcept.gradientText2: Example: If a tissue needs to off-gas 2 bar of nitrogen, switching from air (79% N₂) to Nitrox 50 (50% N₂) or pure O₂ (0% N₂) creates a much larger pressure gradient, so each half-time removes more gas — this is why oxygen-rich mixes accelerate decompression!

halfTimeCharts.title: Interactive: Pressure Delta & Half-Times
halfTimeCharts.intro: These charts demonstrate how the pressure difference affects saturation and desaturation rates.

ongassing.title: On-gassing (Descent)
ongassing.desc: Tissue starts at surface equilibrium (~0.79 bar ppN₂). Adjust target depth to see how bigger pressure differences mean faster absolute loading.

offgassing.title: Off-gassing (Ascent to Surface)
offgassing.desc: Tissue starts saturated at the selected depth. Same half-time, same equation—just inverted. The curves are perfect mirrors.

halfTimeCharts.footnote: ℹ️ Both charts use the same depth and the same half-time formula. On-gassing and off-gassing are symmetrical—only the direction changes.

math.haldaneDesc: When staying at a constant depth, tissue pressure changes according to:
math.pt: tissue N₂ pressure at time t
math.schreinerDesc: During ascent or descent at a constant rate:
math.rDesc: is the rate of change of alveolar pressure (positive for descent).
math.pressureDesc: Every 10 meters of seawater adds approximately 1 bar of pressure.

tissueHeterogeneity.title: Why Different Tissues Behave Differently
tissueHeterogeneity.intro: Your body is not homogenous — different tissues have vastly different characteristics that affect how quickly they absorb and release inert gas:
tissueHeterogeneity.perfusion: Blood perfusion — Well-perfused tissues (brain, heart) exchange gas quickly; poorly-perfused tissues (cartilage, fat) exchange slowly
tissueHeterogeneity.solubility: Gas solubility — Fat dissolves 5× more nitrogen than blood (see table above), so fatty tissues take longer to saturate
tissueHeterogeneity.distance: Distance from blood supply — Gas must diffuse from capillaries into tissue; tissues far from blood supply take longer
tissueHeterogeneity.conclusion: This is why decompression models use multiple theoretical compartments to simulate the full range of tissue behaviors in your body.

buhlmannCompartments.title: Bühlmann's ZH-L16 Compartments
buhlmannCompartments.intro: The Bühlmann ZH-L16 model uses 16 theoretical compartments — these are mathematical constructs fit to experimental data, not literal anatomical tissues. They span a range of half-times designed to model the full spectrum of tissue behaviors:
buhlmannCompartments.fast: Fast compartments (5–12.5 min) — saturate in minutes, but also release gas quickly
buhlmannCompartments.medium: Medium compartments (18.5–77 min) — balance between loading and off-gassing
buhlmannCompartments.slow: Slow compartments (109–635 min) — can take hours to fully saturate
buhlmannCompartments.controlling: At any point during a dive, the controlling compartment is the one closest to its critical supersaturation limit — this compartment determines your decompression ceiling.

zhl16Variants.title: ZH-L16 Variants: A, B, and C
zhl16Variants.intro: Bühlmann developed three variants of the ZH-L16 algorithm, each with different levels of conservatism. The variants differ only in their 'a' coefficients — the half-times and 'b' values remain the same.

a.name: ZH-L16A
a.desc: The original values derived from experimental data. Least conservative — allows the most supersaturation.

b.name: ZH-L16B
b.desc: Modified 'a' values for printed dive tables. More conservative in compartments 5–8 and 13 to account for the inherent rounding in table use.

c.name: ZH-L16C
c.desc: Most conservative — modified 'a' values for compartments 5–15. Since dive computers track depth and time precisely (no table rounding), additional conservatism was added for real-world safety margins.
c.use: 💻 Used for: Dive computers (most common today)

recap.title: What We Know So Far
recap.intro: From the previous sections, we learned about three key pressures and how they relate:
recap.tissueHint: The nitrogen (or helium) dissolved in body tissues
recap.alveolarHint: The ppN₂ in our lungs (≈0.79 × ambient for air)
recap.offgassingDesc: ✅ Off-gassing — nitrogen flows from tissue to lungs. This is good!
recap.supersatDesc: ⚠️ Supersaturation — dissolved gas exceeds what pressure can hold. Bubble risk!
recap.challenge: The challenge: during ascent, we want tissue pressure to exceed alveolar (to off-gas), but we need to limit how much it exceeds ambient pressure (to avoid bubbles).

supersaturation.title: The Supersaturation Problem
supersaturation.text1: When tissue pressure exceeds ambient pressure, we're in a state called supersaturation. Think of it like a carbonated drink—the CO₂ is dissolved under pressure. Open the bottle (reduce pressure) and bubbles form.
supersaturation.text2: The same happens in our tissues if we ascend too fast. But here's the fascinating discovery: the body can tolerate some supersaturation without forming dangerous bubbles. The question is: how much?
supersaturation.haldaneMath: (2 bar → 1 bar, safe from 10m, air only)
supersaturation.workmanDesc: Each compartment has its own limit
supersaturation.historySummary: 📚 The History: How We Discovered Safe Limits
supersaturation.haldaneHistory: The Scottish physiologist observed that workers in compressed-air tunnels and caissons could safely decompress from 2 atmospheres to 1 (a 2:1 ratio). This became the foundation of staged decompression. Note: this 2:1 ratio was derived from experiments with air only — different gas mixtures (trimix, heliox) have different tolerances due to helium's different solubility and diffusion properties.
supersaturation.workmanHistory: U.S. Navy researcher who recognized that a single fixed ratio couldn't capture the full picture. Different tissue compartments tolerate different levels of supersaturation, and these tolerances change with depth. He coined the term "M-value" (Maximum value) — the maximum tolerable tissue inert gas pressure at any given depth. Crucially, Workman developed M-values for both nitrogen and helium (1965), enabling decompression planning for heliox deep dives.
supersaturation.workmanInsight: Workman's key insight: faster tissues (brain, blood) tolerate higher supersaturation than slower tissues (fat, bones) — and the tolerated ratio also varies with depth.

buhlmann.title: Bühlmann's Solution
buhlmann.intro: Swiss physician Prof. Albert A. Bühlmann took this further in his ZH-L16 algorithm. Instead of a single ratio for all tissues, he defined specific tolerance limits for each of the 16 tissue compartments.
buhlmann.coreConceptText: Each tissue compartment has its own M-value line that defines the maximum tolerable tissue pressure for any given ambient pressure. This is the limit—cross it, and bubble formation becomes likely.
buhlmann.fasterTissues: Faster tissues (short half-times like 5 min) → tolerate MORE supersaturation
buhlmann.slowerTissues: Slower tissues (long half-times like 635 min) → tolerate LESS supersaturation
buhlmann.formulaIntro: Bühlmann's M-value formula for each compartment:
buhlmann.formulaM: M = Maximum tolerable tissue inert gas pressure (bar)
buhlmann.formulaHint: The "a" coefficient is the y-intercept — the maximum tolerable tissue pressure at zero gauge pressure (surface). Faster tissues have higher "a" values, meaning they can handle more supersaturation.
buhlmann.variantsSummary: 📚 ZH-L16 Variants: A, B, and C
buhlmann.variantsIntro: Bühlmann published three sets of coefficients:
buhlmann.variantA: ZH-L16A — Mathematically derived from half-times. The original, least conservative set. Used for research.
buhlmann.variantB: ZH-L16B — Slightly more conservative in middle compartments. Designed for printed dive tables (rounded to whole-meter stops).
buhlmann.variantC: ZH-L16C — Most conservative, especially in middle compartments. Designed for real-time dive computers.
buhlmann.variantsHint: Set A was found to be too aggressive for middle compartments in practice, leading to the B and C modifications. Most dive computers today use ZH-L16C.
buhlmann.limitationsText1: M-values are useful but not absolute safety boundaries. Research shows that silent (asymptomatic) bubbles form well within M-value limits — you don't need to cross the line for bubbles to appear.
buhlmann.limitationsText2: Some divers have exceeded M-values without symptoms, while others developed DCS while staying within limits. As Powell puts it: "an M-value can be thought of as a solid black line through a large grey area."
buhlmann.limitationsHint: This is why Gradient Factors exist — to keep tissue loading well below the theoretical M-value limit. See the Gradient Factors page.

diagram.title: The Pressure-Pressure Diagram
diagram.intro: The chart below plots Ambient Pressure (X-axis) against Tissue N₂ Pressure (Y-axis). Watch how your tissue compartments move through the different zones during a dive:
diagram.moveAtDepth: At depth: Stay at same X position, slowly move up toward equilibrium
diagram.moveAscent: Ascent: Move left (↓ ambient) — this is where you enter supersaturation
diagram.movementWarning: ⚠️ The danger: ascending too fast moves you left faster than you off-gas down — risking crossing above the M-value line!

example2.title: Example 2: Ceiling Violation
example2.ceilingText: The ascent ceiling is the shallowest depth you can ascend to without any tissue exceeding its M-value. If you ascend past the ceiling, tissue pressure crosses the M-value line and dangerous bubble formation becomes likely. Decompression stops keep you at or below this ceiling while tissues off-gas.

header.title: Gradient Factors
header.subtitle: Adding conservatism to decompression — and the deep stops debate

greyZone.title: The Grey Zone: Why M-Values Aren't Enough

silentBubbles.title: Silent Bubbles
silentBubbles.text1: Doppler ultrasound studies have revealed something surprising: bubbles form in divers after most dives, even when following conservative profiles with no DCS symptoms.
silentBubbles.insight: These "silent bubbles" (venous gas emboli) are sub-clinical — they don't cause symptoms, but they prove that M-values don't represent a bubble-free boundary. They represent a tolerable level of bubble formation.
silentBubbles.text2: This means the M-value line on our pressure-pressure diagram isn't a sharp "safe/unsafe" boundary. It's more like a probability gradient — the closer you get, the more bubbles form, and the higher your risk.

variability.title: Individual Variability
variability.intro: DCS risk varies enormously between individuals and even between dives for the same person. Factors that increase risk include:
variability.undeservedHit: The term "undeserved hit" describes cases where divers followed all the rules but still got DCS. This happens because we're dealing with probabilistic biology, not precise physics.

discovery.title: Richard Pyle's Discovery
discovery.text1: In the 1980s, Richard Pyle was a marine biologist collecting fish specimens from the "twilight zone" — depths between 50-70 meters. He noticed something curious about his post-dive fatigue.
discovery.insight: The pattern: On dives where he caught fish, he had to stop at intermediate depths to vent their swim bladders (preventing them from bursting during ascent). After these dives, he felt great. On dives with no fish — and therefore no intermediate stops — he felt fatigued.
discovery.text2: Pyle had accidentally discovered that brief stops at depths deeper than required by his decompression schedule made a noticeable difference in how he felt.

method.title: Pyle Stops
method.intro: Pyle formalized his observation into a method:
method.step2: First deep stop = halfway between max depth and first required deco stop
method.step4: If the gap to the next stop is still >9m (30ft), add another halfway stop
method.exampleTitle: Example: 60m dive, first deco stop at 15m
method.vpmConnection: Interestingly, Pyle later discovered that his empirical pattern closely matched the Varying Permeability Model (VPM) — a bubble-based decompression algorithm that independently predicted similar deep stop profiles.

bridge.title: Bridging Pyle's Discovery to Bühlmann
bridge.text1: So Pyle showed that deep stops help, and VPM (a bubble model) explains why. But what if you want to keep using Bühlmann's dissolved-gas model — the algorithm in most dive computers — while still getting those beneficial deep stops?
bridge.text2: That's exactly what Gradient Factors provide. They're a modification to Bühlmann that lets you dial in more conservative profiles, including deeper first stops, without switching to a completely different algorithm.

gfExplained.title: Gradient Factors: The Tool

what.title: What Are Gradient Factors?
what.text1: Gradient Factors (GF) are a way to add conservatism to Bühlmann's algorithm by reducing the allowed supersaturation. Instead of allowing tissues to reach 100% of the M-value, you set a lower percentage.
what.text2: A gradient factor of GF 80% means you only allow the tissue to reach 80% of the way from ambient pressure to the M-value.

gfExplained.sandboxCTA: Open GF sandbox — scrub the formulas live →

lowHigh.title: GF Low and GF High
lowHigh.intro: Dive computers and planning software use two gradient factors:
lowHigh.interpolation: The algorithm interpolates between these values during the ascent:
lowHigh.interpList1: At your deepest required stop → GF Low applies
lowHigh.interpList2: At the surface → GF High applies
lowHigh.insight:
Lower GF Low = deeper first stop (similar to Pyle stops)
Lower GF High = more time at shallow stops

example100.title: Visual: GF 100/100 (No Conservatism)
example100.desc: Raw Bühlmann limits — tissue can reach 100% of M-value.

example5080.title: Visual: GF 50/80 (Conservative)
example5080.desc: Tissue only allowed to 50-80% of M-value — notice the GF line below the M-value.

nedu.cardTitle: The NEDU Study That Changed Everything
nedu.text1: For years, deep stops were considered beneficial based on Pyle's observations and bubble model theory. Then came rigorous testing.
nedu.text2: The U.S. Navy Experimental Diving Unit (NEDU) conducted a large comparative study: same dive (170 fsw/30 min), same total decompression time, but different profiles:
nedu.result: Deep stops resulted in 3.6× more DCS for the same dive!

backfire.title: Why Deep Stops Can Backfire
backfire.text1: The problem with deep stops is subtle but important:
backfire.insight: At deep stop depths, slow tissues are still on-gassing. While you're trying to let fast tissues off-gas, you're loading up the slow tissues that will control your later decompression.
backfire.text2: Deep stops reduce the pressure gradient for off-gassing. The deeper you stay, the smaller the difference between tissue pressure and ambient — and that gradient is what drives gas elimination.
backfire.nuanceIntro: This doesn't mean all deep stops are bad:
backfire.nuance1: Very brief stops (Pyle's original 2-3 minutes) may still be beneficial
backfire.nuance2: The NEDU study used extended deep stops with significant deco time shifted deep
backfire.nuance3: Extremely aggressive deep stop profiles (GF 30/85) are now discouraged
backfire.nuance4: Moderate conservatism (GF 70/85) adds safety without excessive deep stops

settings.title: Gradient Factors — decompression conservatism settings
settings.noteGfLow: determines the depth of the first deco stop and influences deeper stops
settings.noteGfHigh: influences shallow-stop time and overall surfacing time
settings.row4depth: take a longer break from diving
settings.credit: Reference table courtesy of Jirka Hovorka.

ratio.title: The Ratio Rule
ratio.intro: Decompression researcher Dr. David Doolette suggests a practical guideline:
ratio.insight: GF Low should be approximately 83% of GF High
ratio.insightDesc: This ratio matches the average Bühlmann 'b' parameter and avoids over-emphasizing deep stops.

bottomLine.title: The Bottom Line
bottomLine.item1: Some conservatism is good — GF 100/100 is too aggressive
bottomLine.item2: GF 70/85 is a sensible starting point for most divers
bottomLine.item3: Very low GF Low (like 30%) can be counterproductive
bottomLine.item4: More conservatism isn't always better — it's about balance
bottomLine.item5: Adjust based on personal factors, dive conditions, and experience

cmas.title: What CMAS recommends (2025)
cmas.intro: CMAS published a 2025 fact sheet summarising current evidence on gradient factors. Its advice differs from some of the values in the reference table above — worth knowing both perspectives before you pick your settings.

pointSymmetric.title: 1. For air/nitrox, use symmetric GFs
pointSymmetric.text: CMAS recommends GF Low = GF High on nitrogen dives — typically 90/90, dropping to 85/85 or 80/80 when risk factors apply (age, fatigue, cold, exertion). Asymmetric GFs force deep stops, and multiple independent studies found this increases DCS incidence on air/nitrox dives:
pointSymmetric.bullet1: French Navy (2005) — deep stops raised DCS risk on air deco dives
pointSymmetric.bullet2: U.S. Navy NEDU (2011) — "redistribution of stop time from shallow to deep stops increases incidence of DCS in air decompression dives"
pointSymmetric.bullet3: Belgian Military (2023) — default 30/70 preset was unsafe for 60 m air dives

pointHelium.title: 2. For helium (trimix/heliox), asymmetric GFs are still justified
pointHelium.text: On helium mixes, forcing some deeper stops does help (inner-ear DCS, fast helium tissues). CMAS suggests GF Low 30–50, GF High 70–80 (e.g. 30/70, 50/80). This aligns with the "Deep dive" row of the table above.

pointNoStop.title: 3. On a no-deco dive, GF Low doesn't matter
pointNoStop.text: Non-obvious but important: GF Low only kicks in at the first deco stop depth. If your dive has no mandatory stops, setting 45/95 behaves exactly like 95/95 — because there is no "first stop" for GF Low to anchor. Don't expect conservative GF Low to help you on a pure recreational profile.

pointDefaults.title: 4. Check your computer's default preset
pointDefaults.text: Many dive computers ship with GF 30/70 out of the box — a preset chosen for tech/trimix diving. CMAS argues the same preset is not right for air/nitrox.

beyond.title: Beyond Dissolved Gas
beyond.text: Bühlmann's algorithm only tracks dissolved gas. It doesn't model bubble formation or growth. Alternative "bubble models" attempt to address this.

vpm.title: VPM (Varying Permeability Model)
vpm.text1: VPM assumes that microscopic bubble nuclei always exist in tissues. During decompression, nuclei larger than a "critical radius" (determined by max depth) will grow.
vpm.text2: VPM aims to minimize total bubble volume by keeping ambient pressure high enough to limit bubble growth — naturally producing deeper stops.

rgbm.title: RGBM (Reduced Gradient Bubble Model)
rgbm.text: RGBM models how bubbles grow by acquiring gas from surrounding saturated tissue. Like VPM, it tends to produce deeper stops than Bühlmann.

realityCheck.title: The Reality Check
realityCheck.text: Despite different theoretical foundations, all these algorithms produce surprisingly similar schedules — because they all must match the same empirical data from real dives.
realityCheck.quote: "It is far too easy to look at the complexity of any calculation, and the number of decimal places that a modern computer will display, and get the impression that the result is extremely accurate when in fact it is not."

gfChart.formulaIntro: Instantaneous Gradient Factor for a tissue at ambient pressure P<sub>amb</sub>:
gfChart.formulaMValue: Bühlmann M-value at Pamb: M(Pamb) = a + Pamb / b
gfChart.varAB: a, b — ZH-L16 Bühlmann coefficients for that tissue
gfChart.varGF: GF — 0 % at ambient (fully saturated, no gradient), 100 % at the M-value (Bühlmann limit)
gfChart.rampNote: During ascent the allowed GF is ramped linearly from GF Low at the pAnchor depth to GF High at the surface. The green corridor in the chart shows that allowed region.

disclaimer.text: Educational Use Only — This tool demonstrates Gay-Lussac's Law for rigid scuba cylinders.

header.title: Gas Law: Temperature & Pressure
header.subtitle: How temperature changes affect pressure in a rigid scuba cylinder (Gay-Lussac's Law)

gasLaw.calculatePrompt: Set up your scenario, calculate P<sub>2</sub>, then click below to check your answer.

safety.aboveWorking: Above working pressure! {0} bar (test pressure: {1} bar)
safety.danger: DANGER! {0} bar exceeds test pressure ({1} bar)

gasLaw.whyText1: Gas molecules move faster at higher temperatures and hit the cylinder walls harder, increasing pressure. Since the cylinder is rigid (constant volume), all the extra kinetic energy translates directly to higher pressure.
gasLaw.whyText2: Practical tip: Compressors generate significant heat during filling — gas inside a freshly filled cylinder can be 40–50°C above ambient. If you fill to 200 bar in a warm shop and dive in a cold lake, don't be surprised to see only ~180 bar on your gauge. That's not a leak — it's physics.
gasLaw.whyRuleOfThumb: Rule of thumb: ~0.6 bar change per 1°C at 200 bar working pressure.
gasLaw.formulaNote: pressure / temperature ratio is constant at constant volume (T in Kelvin)

footer.text: Disclaimer: For educational purposes only. Based on ideal gas law assumptions.

quote.text: "There is a false sense of security amongst recreational divers that decompression is a well understood science and that decompression illness can easily be avoided if you stick to your decompression tables."

topics.gradientFactorsDesc: Explore how GF Low and GF High settings add conservatism to your decompression schedule.

what.title: What Is This?
what.body: This is an interactive educational resource for divers who want to understand the science behind their dive computers. All visualizations are based on the Bühlmann ZH-L16 decompression model, one of the most widely used algorithms in recreational and technical diving.
what.goal: The goal is to make abstract concepts like tissue saturation, half-times, and M-values more intuitive through hands-on exploration and visualization.

algo.title: Algorithm Details
algo.intro: The decompression calculations use the Bühlmann ZH-L16 algorithm with the following parameters and assumptions:

variants.title: Model Variants
variants.a: ZH-L16A: Original experimental values, TC1 half-time = 4.0 min
variants.b: ZH-L16B: Modified for printed tables, TC1 half-time = 5.0 min
variants.c: ZH-L16C: Modified for dive computers (default), TC1 half-time = 5.0 min

constants.title: Constants
constants.waterVapor: Water vapor pressure: 0.0627 bar (47 mmHg at 37°C)

gf.title: Gradient Factors
gf.intro: Gradient factors use the Baker pAnchor method:
gf.item1: GF Low applies at the pAnchor depth (first stop)
gf.item2: Linear interpolation from pAnchor to surface (GF High)

equations.title: Equations
equations.haldane: Haldane equation: Tissue loading at constant depth
equations.schreiner: Schreiner equation: Tissue loading during depth changes

validation.title: Validation
validation.intro: The implementation has been validated against:
validation.buhlmann: Bühlmann printed tables: Deco schedules match within expected tolerance
validation.note: Note: Our calculations may produce 10-25% shorter deco times than printed tables. This is expected — printed tables include safety margins and round up conservatively. This tool shows the raw algorithm output for educational purposes.

refs.title: 📖 References & Sources
refs.item1: Jahns, Jan. (2008). Fyzika. Svaz českých potápěčů, Praha. — Comprehensive overview of diving physics for experienced divers and instructors. Covers essential topics with practical examples from diving. Review on Strany potápěčské
refs.item2: Jahns, Jan. (2008). Podklady k výpočtům dekompresních tabulek Bühlmann/SUSV 1986. 2. vydání. Hlučín, 34 stran. — Mathematical foundations of the Bühlmann ZH-L16 decompression model, including saturation/desaturation equations, M-values, deco stop calculations, and a supplement on ZH-L16B with gradient factors and trimix extensions. Full text (PDF, SPMS)
refs.item3: Powell, Mark. Deco for Divers. — The primary inspiration for this project. An excellent, accessible guide to decompression theory for recreational and technical divers. Highly recommended!
refs.item4: Bühlmann, A.A. (1984). Decompression–Decompression Sickness. Berlin: Springer-Verlag. — The original work describing the ZH-L16 algorithm.
refs.item5: Wikipedia. Bühlmann decompression algorithm — Overview of the algorithm, tissue compartment half-times, and M-values.
refs.item6: Wienke, B.R. Decompression Theory (PDF) — Comprehensive introduction to decompression physics and physiology.
refs.item7: Alveolar Gas Equation: The model accounts for water vapor pressure at body temperature (37°C) = 47 mmHg ≈ 0.0627 bar, which reduces the effective partial pressure of inspired gases. Wikipedia: Alveolar gas equation
refs.item8: Schreiner, H.R. (1971). Safe Limits of Exposure to Increased Pressure. — Derivation of the Schreiner equation for calculating gas loading during linear pressure changes.
refs.item9: Strany potápěčské. stranypotapecske.cz — A comprehensive Czech diving portal and community resource run by Zdeněk Šraier. Features an extensive library of book reviews, educational articles on diving physics and decompression theory, dive site conditions database, equipment reviews, and training materials. An invaluable resource for Czech-speaking divers at all levels.

privacy.title: Privacy Policy
privacy.subtitle: How decotheory.eu and the DecoTheory mobile app handle your data

summary.title: Short version
summary.text: Both this website and the DecoTheory mobile app store all data locally on your device. Neither transmits data to any server. There is no analytics, no crash reporting, no advertising, no account system, and no third-party SDKs that collect data.

web.title: Website (decotheory.eu)
web.localStorage: Uses browser localStorage to remember your dive setups, quiz progress, and language preference. This data never leaves your browser.
web.serviceWorker: A service worker caches the site's HTML, CSS, and JavaScript so it works offline. The cache lives only in your browser; you can clear it at any time via your browser's settings.
web.thirdParty: External links (e.g. to Wikipedia, GitHub, Strany potápěčské) are loaded only when you click them, never automatically.

mobile.title: DecoTheory mobile app
mobile.asyncStorage: Uses AsyncStorage to remember your diver profile, dive plans, and quiz progress. This data is stored only on your device.
mobile.permissions: Requires no Android permissions beyond what Expo SDK 54 includes by default for app installation.
mobile.uninstall: Uninstalling the app removes all locally stored data.
mobile.deepLinks: The decotheory:// deep-link scheme is used only for sharing plans between the app and this website. No data is sent to any server.

notdone.title: What we explicitly do NOT do
notdone.analytics: No analytics or telemetry of any kind.
notdone.sdks: No third-party SDKs that collect data.
notdone.backend: No server backend that sees your activity.

contact.title: Contact

palv.name: P<sub>alv</sub> | alveolar N<sub>2</sub> pressure
palv.why: What the lungs are pushing into the blood at target depth.

pt0.name: P<sub>t,0</sub> | tissue pressure at t=0
pt0.why: Where this compartment started, assumed equilibrated at start depth.

k.name: k | rate constant
k.why: Faster compartments → bigger k → catch up sooner.

exp.name: e<sup>−kt</sup> | "fraction left to go"
exp.why: 1.0 at t=0, decays toward 0. Half-gone every T½.

schreiner.title: Schreiner Equation
schreiner.subtitle: Linear-rate companion to the Haldane page — watch the equation evolve as ambient pressure slides.
schreiner.disclaimerBanner: Educational Use Only — Interactive walk-through of the Schreiner equation for linear-rate ambient pressure changes.
schreiner.disclaimer: Disclaimer: For educational purposes only. The actual diving algorithm uses additional logic.

labels.depthRate: Depth rate (m/min, positive = descending ↓, negative = ascending ↑)

palv0.name: P<sub>alv,0</sub> | alveolar N<sub>2</sub> at start depth
palv0.why: Starting alveolar pressure. Slope-zero point of the moving alveolar source.

pt0.name: P<sub>t,0</sub> | tissue pressure at t=0
pt0.why: Tissue assumed equilibrated at start depth → equals P<sub>alv,0</sub>.

r.name: R | alveolar pressure rate
r.why: Positive = descent (alveolar climbing), negative = ascent. R = 0 → equation collapses to Haldane.

k.name: k | rate constant
k.why: Faster compartments → bigger k → catch up sooner.

exp.name: e<sup>−kt</sup> | exponential decay factor
exp.why: 1.0 at t=0, decays toward 0. Multiplied by the initial-disequilibrium term.

moving.name: Moving alveolar source
moving.why: Where the alveolar source is right now (linear in t).

lag.name: Phase lag (R/k)
lag.why: How far below (ascent) or above (descent) the source a perfectly-tracking tissue would settle. Equivalent to 1/k minutes of slope.

decay.name: Decaying initial gap
decay.why: The initial offset between actual Pt and the tracking line — settles exponentially toward zero.

mvalues.title: M-Values
mvalues.subtitle: Where the line comes from, and what it looks like for all 16 compartments.
mvalues.disclaimerBanner: Educational Use Only — Interactive walk-through of Bühlmann's M-value formula and where its coefficients come from.
mvalues.disclaimer: Disclaimer: For educational purposes only. The actual diving algorithm uses additional logic.

top.heading: What does M look like at this depth?
top.anchor: Pick a depth, a compartment, and a variant — see Bühlmann's M-value formula evaluate live.

a.name: a | tissue intercept
a.why: Y-intercept of the M-line. Higher = more supersaturation tolerated at the surface.

pAmb.name: P<sub>amb</sub> | ambient pressure
pAmb.why: The horizontal axis of the M-line. Each meter of depth adds 0.1 bar.

b.name: b | tissue slope
b.why: Lower b → steeper M-line → faster compartment.

m.name: M | tolerated tissue pressure
m.why: Above this, the algorithm flags supersaturation as unsafe.

bottom.heading: Where do a and b come from?
bottom.anchor: ZH-L16A's a and b aren't fitted to data — they're computed from half-time alone. Variants B and C are post-hoc adjustments to specific compartments.

halfTime.name: t<sub>½</sub> | half-time
halfTime.why: Each compartment's signature time. Not anatomical — a sample point on an exponential axis.

a.name: a(t<sub>½</sub>) | analytical intercept
a.why: Variants B and C drop a for specific compartments — that's the only place statistics enter Bühlmann.

b.name: b(t<sub>½</sub>) | analytical slope
b.why: Identical across A/B/C except TC1 (whose t½ swap also swaps b).

gradientFactors.title: Gradient Factors
gradientFactors.subtitle: Three formulas, one ramp. Scrub the sliders and watch the wiki's GF math come to life.
gradientFactors.wipNote: 🚧 Work in progress — experimental playground. Feedback welcome.
gradientFactors.disclaimer: Disclaimer: For educational purposes only. The actual diving algorithm uses additional logic (multi-compartment search for the controlling tissue, gas-switch-aware pAnchor derivation, etc.).

controls.heading: Controls
controls.anchorHint: Teaching knob — scrub to see the ramp tilt. In a real dive, pAnchor is derived from tissue state, not chosen.

warnings.inverted: ⚠ GF Lo > GF Hi — the ramp is inverted. Real dives never run this way.

ceiling.name: Ceiling
ceiling.violation: Ceiling above current depth — ascending here would violate the limit

a.why: Y-intercept of the M-line for the selected compartment + variant. Higher = more supersaturation tolerated.

b.why: Slope is 1/b. Smaller b → steeper line → faster compartment.

gfLo.name: GF Lo
gfLo.why: Fraction of the supersaturation budget allowed at the first stop. Lower = deeper first stop.

gfHi.name: GF Hi
gfHi.why: Fraction of the budget allowed at the surface. Lower = more conservative surfacing.

pAnchor.name: pAnchor
pAnchor.why: Ambient pressure of the first deco stop. The point where GF clamps at GF Lo.

mAdj.name: M_adj
mAdj.why: GF-adjusted limit: at GF=0 it collapses onto the ambient line, at GF=1 onto the raw M-line. In between it's a line that pivots between those two — slope sits between 1 and 1/b.
